title: Neural signalling
summary: How neurons generate and conduct electrical impulses and pass signals across synapses, and (HL) how ion channels, summation and drugs shape what the nervous system does.

keyterms.definition: A cell of the nervous system that carries electrical impulses; it has a cell body, many short dendrites and a single long axon.
The potential difference across the membrane of a neuron not conducting an impulse, about −70 mV (inside negative).
A membrane pump using ATP to move Na+ out and K+ into the neuron, establishing and maintaining concentration gradients of both ions.
A rapid depolarization and repolarization of a neuron's membrane that is propagated along the nerve fibre as a nerve impulse.
A change in membrane potential from negative towards positive, caused by positive ions (Na+) entering the neuron.
Layers of membrane wrapped around a nerve fibre, insulating it and increasing the speed of impulse conduction.
A junction between two neurons, or between a neuron and an effector cell, across which signals pass chemically in one direction.
A neurotransmitter, used at many synapses including neuromuscular junctions, that is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.
A depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by a neurotransmitter opening positive-ion channels.
An ion channel that opens or closes in response to changes in membrane potential; voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels produce action potentials.
The membrane potential (about −50 mV) that must be reached for voltage-gated Na+ channels to open and an action potential to occur.
Diffusion of Na+ ions along the axon from a depolarized region to the adjacent resting region, depolarizing it to threshold.
Conduction in myelinated fibres in which action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps from node to node.
A hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by an inhibitory neurotransmitter, making an action potential less likely.
The combining of excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials; an action potential is fired only if the total reaches the threshold.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a neuron to its description.

pairs.right: Many short fibres that receive signals
Single long fibre that carries impulses away
Insulating layer that speeds up conduction

questions.explanation: Signals are received by dendrites, integrated near the cell body, and carried along the axon; myelin increases conduction speed.

questions.prompt: How is the resting potential generated?
options: Na+ diffuses into the neuron through open channels
Negative ions are pumped out of the neuron
The Na+/K+ pump moves Na+ out and K+ in using ATP, and K+ leaks out, leaving the inside negative
Ca2+ ions enter the axon from the synapse
questions.explanation: The pump establishes gradients (Na+ high outside, K+ high inside). The membrane is more permeable to K+, so K+ leaks out, leaving the inside negative at about −70 mV.

questions.text: A typical resting potential is about ___ mV.
questions.explanation: At rest the inside of the neuron is about 70 mV more negative than the outside. +30 mV is the peak of an action potential; −50 mV is about the threshold.

questions.statement: At resting potential, the inside of the axon is positive relative to the outside.
questions.explanation: At rest the inside is negative (about −70 mV). It only becomes positive briefly during the depolarization phase of an action potential.

questions.prompt: What is a nerve impulse?
options: An action potential: a rapid depolarization and repolarization that travels along the nerve fibre
A flow of electrons along the axon, as in a wire
A neurotransmitter moving along the axon
A permanent change in resting potential
questions.explanation: Impulses are electrical because they involve movement of positive ions across the membrane, not electrons; each region depolarizes and repolarizes in turn.

questions.statement: Myelinated nerve fibres conduct impulses faster than non-myelinated fibres of the same diameter.
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the fibre so the impulse jumps between gaps in the myelin, which is much faster than depolarizing every part of the membrane.

questions.prompt: Squid giant axons are not myelinated, yet they conduct impulses quickly. Why?
options: They have more Na+/K+ pumps
They are shorter than other axons
They contain more acetylcholine
Their very large diameter reduces resistance to ion flow
questions.explanation: Conduction speed increases with axon diameter. The squid's giant axon gives a fast escape response; vertebrates achieve high speeds in thinner fibres by myelination.

questions.text: The sodium–potassium pump uses energy from ___ to move ions against their concentration gradients.
questions.explanation: The pump is active transport: each cycle uses one ATP to pump 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a neuron in the order a signal passes through them.
questions.explanation: Dendrites receive signals, the cell body integrates them, the axon conducts the impulse, and the axon terminal releases neurotransmitter at a synapse.

questions.prompt: A scatter graph of impulse speed against axon diameter has R² = 0.92. What can be concluded?
options: Increasing diameter is proven to cause faster impulses
There is a strong positive correlation, but this alone does not prove causation
There is no relationship between the variables
92% of axons are myelinated
questions.explanation: R² measures how well the trend line fits: 0.92 means a strong correlation. A correlation alone does not establish cause; a mechanism or controlled experiment is needed.

questions.prompt: Why do chemical synapses transmit signals in one direction only?
options: Postsynaptic neurons cannot generate action potentials
Action potentials can only move towards the cell body
Neurotransmitter is released only by the presynaptic neuron, and receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane
The synaptic cleft is filled with myelin
questions.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only in the presynaptic terminal, and receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal can only pass one way.

questions.prompt: Put the events of synaptic transmission in order.
items: An action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane
Calcium ions diffuse into the presynaptic terminal
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft
Neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Na+ ions enter and the postsynaptic membrane depolarizes
questions.explanation: Depolarization triggers Ca2+ uptake, which triggers exocytosis; neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors, opening positive-ion channels.

questions.statement: Neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic membrane by exocytosis.
questions.explanation: Vesicles containing neurotransmitter fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents into the synaptic cleft.

questions.text: Acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft is broken down by the enzyme ___.
questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses acetylcholine in the cleft, ending its effect so the postsynaptic membrane can repolarize.

questions.prompt: What directly triggers vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane?
options: Uptake of calcium ions into the presynaptic terminal
Binding of acetylcholine to the presynaptic membrane
Efflux of potassium ions
Breakdown of acetylcholine
questions.explanation: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane causes calcium ions to diffuse in, and the rise in Ca2+ causes vesicles to fuse and release neurotransmitter.

questions.statement: Synapses are only found between two neurons.
questions.explanation: Synapses also form between neurons and effector cells, such as muscle fibres at neuromuscular junctions or gland cells.

questions.prompt: How does acetylcholine generate an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
options: It enters the postsynaptic cell and releases electrons
It hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
It activates the Na+/K+ pump
It binds to receptors that open channels, allowing Na+ to enter and depolarize the membrane
questions.explanation: Binding opens positive-ion channels; Na+ diffuses in, depolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. If this reaches threshold, an action potential follows.

questions.prompt: Match each substance to its role at a cholinergic synapse.

pairs.right: Enter presynaptic terminal and trigger exocytosis
Binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Hydrolyses acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft

questions.explanation: Ca2+ couples the impulse to release; acetylcholine carries the signal; Na+ entry produces the EPSP; acetylcholinesterase ends the signal.

questions.text: A synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre is a neuromuscular ___.
questions.explanation: At neuromuscular junctions acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter; it depolarizes the muscle fibre membrane, leading to contraction.

questions.prompt: Why must acetylcholine be removed rapidly from the synaptic cleft?
options: So it can be pumped back into the blood
Otherwise the postsynaptic membrane would remain depolarized and keep being stimulated
Because it is toxic to presynaptic neurons
So the presynaptic neuron can reach threshold
questions.explanation: Rapid breakdown by acetylcholinesterase allows the postsynaptic cell to repolarize, so each impulse gives a discrete response.

questions.prompt: Put the events of an action potential in order.
items: Membrane is depolarized to the threshold potential
Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ diffuses in
Inside of the membrane becomes positive (about +30 mV)
Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open
K+ diffuses out, repolarizing the membrane
Na+/K+ pump restores the ion gradients
questions.explanation: Na+ influx causes depolarization; K+ efflux causes repolarization. The pump then restores the concentration gradients for the next impulse.

questions.prompt: What happens if a stimulus does not depolarize the membrane to the threshold potential?
options: A smaller action potential is produced
No action potential is produced
The membrane hyperpolarizes permanently
K+ channels open instead
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-nothing: unless threshold (about −50 mV) is reached, voltage-gated Na+ channels do not open in large numbers.

questions.text: Repolarization occurs when voltage-gated ___ channels open.
questions.explanation: K+ ions diffuse out down their concentration gradient, making the inside negative again.

questions.prompt: How do local currents propagate an action potential along an axon?
options: Na+ ions diffuse along the inside of the axon to the next region, depolarizing it to threshold
K+ ions are pumped along the axon by active transport
Neurotransmitter diffuses along the axon
Electrons flow through the myelin sheath
questions.explanation: Na+ entering at the active region diffuses to the adjacent resting region, raising its potential to threshold so its Na+ channels open.

questions.statement: In myelinated fibres, action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier.
questions.explanation: Ion pumps and channels are clustered at the nodes, and myelin prevents ion movement elsewhere, so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction).

questions.prompt: An oscilloscope trace shows 12 action potentials in 0.5 s. What is the frequency of impulses?
options: 6 per second
12 per second
24 per second
48 per second
questions.explanation: 12 impulses ÷ 0.5 s = 24 impulses per second. Stronger stimuli give a higher frequency of impulses, not bigger impulses.

questions.prompt: Match each chemical to its effect on synaptic transmission.

pairs.right: Bind insect acetylcholine receptors, blocking transmission

questions.explanation: Neonicotinoids are not broken down by acetylcholinesterase, so receptors stay blocked and insects are paralysed. Cocaine leaves dopamine in the cleft, causing excess stimulation.

questions.statement: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.explanation: An IPSP hyperpolarizes the membrane (makes it more negative), moving it further from threshold, so an action potential is less likely.

questions.prompt: A postsynaptic neuron receives EPSPs from several neurons and IPSPs from others. When will it fire an action potential?
options: Whenever any EPSP arrives
Only if no IPSPs arrive
Only if more neurons are excitatory than inhibitory
Only if the summed effect of all inputs depolarizes the membrane to threshold
questions.explanation: Summation combines all excitatory and inhibitory inputs; the outcome is all-or-nothing, depending on whether threshold is reached.

questions.text: Free nerve endings in the skin have channels opened by high temperature, acid, or ___ from chilli peppers.
questions.explanation: These channels let positive ions in, depolarizing the sensory neuron; impulses travel to the brain, where pain is perceived.

questions.prompt: Why is consciousness described as an emergent property?
options: It arises from interactions among many neurons rather than from any single neuron
It is produced by one specialized neuron type
It is coded by a single gene
It is a property of each individual synapse
questions.explanation: An emergent property appears at a higher level of organization from interactions of the parts; no single neuron is conscious.

questions.prompt: How does cocaine affect synapses that use dopamine?
options: It breaks down dopamine in the cleft
It blocks the release of dopamine
It blocks dopamine reuptake, so dopamine stays in the cleft and stimulation is prolonged
It hyperpolarizes the presynaptic membrane
questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks the transporters that take dopamine back into the presynaptic neuron, so dopamine accumulates and keeps stimulating postsynaptic receptors.
